title: Cables Under the Sea: How the Internet Travels
summary: How almost all internet data between countries travels as light through glass fibers in cables on the ocean floor, how the cables are protected, laid, and repaired, and how they link Saudi Arabia to the world.
poll: Most of the internet travels through space.

versions.title: Cables in the Sea
versions.text:
You send a pic to a friend. Your friend is far, far away. How does it get there? It goes in the sea!

The internet does not go up to space. Most of it runs in long cables. The cables lie on the sea floor. They link land to land.

A cable has glass in it. The glass is as thin as a hair. Light zips in the glass. The light takes your words and pics. It is so fast!

Deep down, a cable is as thick as a hose. Near the shore, it is much bigger. It has a coat of steel. The coat keeps it safe. Ships drop big hooks. Boats drag nets. The coat helps.

Light gets weak on a long trip. So small boxes on the cable make it strong.

A big ship lays the cable. It drops it in the sea bit by bit. If a cable breaks, a ship comes to fix it.

The first sea cable was laid in 1858. It did not last long.

Some cables come up at Jeddah, on the Red Sea. They link us to the world.

versions.title: Cables Under the Sea
versions.text:
You send a photo to a friend in a far land. It gets there in a flash. How? It goes under the sea!

Most of the internet does not fly through space. It runs through long cables. The cables lie on the sea floor. They link one land to the next.

Each cable has strands of glass in it. Each strand is as thin as a hair. Light zips through the glass. The light carries your words, songs, and photos. It moves very fast.

In deep water, a cable is as thick as a garden hose. Near the shore, it is much thicker. It has a coat of steel wires. The coat keeps it safe from ship anchors and fishing nets.

Light gets weak on a long trip. So the cable has small boxes along the way. They make the light strong again.

A big ship lays the cable. It drops the cable into the sea, bit by bit. If a cable breaks, a ship comes to fix it.

The first cable across a big sea was laid in 1858. It broke down in just a few weeks.

Some of these cables come up on land at Jeddah, by the Red Sea. They help link Saudi Arabia to the rest of the world.

HIGH.prompt: Undersea cables are described as vulnerable. Explain why they are vulnerable and how people protect and repair them, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained why the cables are vulnerable.
I described at least two ways people protect or repair them.
I used evidence and key words from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Undersea cables are vulnerable because, even though they transmit optical signals as flashes of light, in deep water they are only as thick as a garden hose, and most damage comes from ship anchors and fishing nets catching on them. To protect the cables, engineers add steel armor near the shore where ships and fishing gear are more likely to snag them, and repeaters placed every 50 to 100 kilometers amplify the weakening light signal along the way. When a cable does break, a repair ship lifts the damaged section to the surface so workers can splice the fiber back together and restore the connection.
